speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: asked	the Minister for Manpower in light of the Q2 2016 Labour Market report wherein it is indicated that there is a rise in the unemployment rate, a lower rate of re-entry and the number of unemployed persons has now outnumbered job vacancies, what is the Ministry doing to (i) overcome these three trends, including youth unemployment; (ii) help the unemployed, especially the vulnerable who have a lower re-entry rate; and (iii) minimise the skill/job/expectation mismatches that have contributed to their unemployment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked	the Minister for Manpower (a) why the rate of employment among locals has remained stagnant over the past 18 months despite the tightening on foreign manpower supply; and (b) what is being done to address and overcome this trend.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: asked	the Minister for Manpower with the number of redundancies and retrenchment cases reaching record levels in the first half of 2016, how will the Ministry (i) help affected workers, especially the PMETs, who are the most affected; (ii) assist lower wage workers to find alternative employment quickly; and (iii) prepare our workers for new jobs in industries facing poor economic prospects.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked	the Minister for Manpower (a) whether there will be a further rise in job losses in the next 12 months; (b) what are the sectors that are likely to be more impacted; and (c) whether is there a need to tighten up Employment Passes and S Passes as more local PMETs become available due to increasing job losses and slower job growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: asked	the Minister for Manpower whether the Government will review the Employment Pass scheme in light of increasing redundancies affecting PMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: asked	the Minister for Manpower (a) whether there will be enhanced efforts by the various job placement agencies to assist with job matching services for local workers who are retrenched or jobseekers who have been unsuccessful in their job search efforts; (b) what is the Ministry's assessment of employers' readiness level in supporting these efforts; and (c) what can employers do to make job vacancies and requirements known to jobseekers beyond listing on the national Jobs Bank.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked	the Minister for Manpower (a) whether the Ministry has any plans to better help retrenched local workers, particularly PMETs, in their job searching process; and (b) whether the list of Professional Conversion Programmes can be expanded to cover more industries and sectors so that PMETs can have more career options.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: asked the Minister for Manpower what programmes and initiatives have been created to assist Singaporeans to secure employment and to encourage companies and employers to create new job vocations and opportunities in the present economic climate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: asked	the Minister for Manpower (a) to date this year, how many PMETs under 40 years of age have been made redundant; (b) what is the rationale to restrict the Career Support Programme for PMETs to those who have been unemployed for six months or more; and (c) whether this restriction to access the programme should be removed for PMETs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Minister for Manpower whether the Ministry will consider upgrading the national Jobs Bank to a national Jobs Registry by (i) making it mandatory for employers to advertise all job openings in parallel within the national Jobs Bank even if the job opening has been advertised through other platforms; and (ii) requiring employers to report hiring outcomes to the Ministry.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked	the Minister for Manpower what measures are in place to help displaced workers with new job opportunities and to create more quality jobs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: asked	the Minister for Manpower how are e2i and other relevant job matching agencies beefing up their effort to help Singaporeans find suitable jobs, especially those affected by job redundancy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Today, my reply would not be 12 times longer.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, I will take slightly longer and I hope Members will please bear with me.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Why did the sharp drop in local employment growth not lead to a sharp rise in unemployment rate?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We saw more people left employment after termination and completion of contract and casual employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: More also left to pursue further studies and upgrading.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But the swing was also structural, across all age groups.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For those aged 25-64, our labour force participation rate of 83.1% is already high and showing signs of plateauing.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the younger ones aged 15-24, the size of the cohort entering the labour force had already peaked in 2013 and started to decline since then.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: More importantly, the number of people retiring is also on the rise, doubling over the last two years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This will continue as more baby boomers enter retirement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In short, even though the numbers of exits and entries in our local workforce will fluctuate from year to year due to prevailing economic conditions and policy factors, but with ageing and lower birth rates, coupled with our relatively high labour force participation rate and low unemployment rate, we will see a continued slowdown of local labour force growth, towards negligible levels, or even stagnation in the next decade.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, we must work our way towards healthier economic growth.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Even though flat local employment growth in the past 18 months did not lead to a sharp rise in unemployment rate or any drop in our labour force participation, we are still concerned that this could still happen if the global economic situation does not improve or worsen further.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must make sure that the current low growth of 1%-2% is transitional.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our future norm should be 2%-3% of quality growth, not 1%-2% of low growth.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is because our ultimate objective in pursuing growth is not in growth itself, but to create jobs in sufficient quantity and of good enough quality for our people to have better jobs, better wages and better careers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Even though local employment went up by only 700, but the number of locals looking for jobs was many times higher than that.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must not forget that there were actually 190,000 new entries of young locals and re-entries of mature locals in that year alone.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Many of them were not just looking for the same jobs vacated by those who have left employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With better education and skills profile, they wanted better jobs to meet their higher expectations and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The same also applies to those who were already in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is also why we can never slow down.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To move faster, we have mobilised industry leaders, unions and economic agencies to create and re-create many more quality jobs in more than 20 sectors, as explained by Minister Lim Hng Kiang and Minister Iswaran.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have to make sure that this innovative growth of our future 	Page: 36 economy will also be an inclusive growth for all our people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At one extreme, if we try to make up for the drop in local labour force growth by taking in many more foreign workers, the pace of our restructuring will slow.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Eventually, we will become overly reliant on foreign manpower and our wages will also stagnate without productivity gain.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the other extreme, if we try to reduce the growth of foreign manpower to zero, zero local labour force growth plus zero foreign manpower growth will give us zero growth in total labour force.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And if labour productivity growth continues to remain at the current level – then zero growth in local workforce, zero growth in foreign manpower, plus zero growth in productivity as we have seen in recent years – it will give us zero growth in our GDP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our economy will eventually stagnate, too, and we obviously cannot allow this to happen.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is why we are transforming our industries for higher productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We need to move towards higher productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, we are adopting a balanced approach in managing the inflow of foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are increasingly more selective in terms of qualifications and experience of the individual foreigners.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, more importantly, to ensure that our people are treated fairly at all levels in all industries, we have included the adoption of fair and progressive HR practices as part of our Work Pass criteria.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This balanced approach will enable our combined workforce of locals and foreigners to complement each other better and compete more aggressively for good investments globally, such as the opening of Micron's expanded facility here last month, as cited by Minister Iswaran.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We need to compete and win many more of such good investments so that we can keep creating better quality growth for the economy and, more importantly, better quality jobs for our people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are doing more to help our workers in this period of economic transition in terms of training support, wage support, job search and career conversion.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In response to Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Ang Wei Neng, Mr Ang Hin Kee, Mr Christopher de Souza, Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Desmond Choo, we have stepped up job matching and career services with the introduction of the Adapt and Grow initiative this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The number of successful job placements is also much more than last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, of the 13,000 successful jobseekers, 45% of 	Page: 37 them, or 5,700, were PMETs, and 55%, or 7,300, were rank-and-file workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They came from various age groups – one in three were below 40 years old, one in four between 40 and 49, and 40%, or two in five, were aged 50 and above.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, we are helping not just the younger workers but also helping the middle-aged as well as the mature workers to secure jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are doing more for the rank-and-file workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We stepped up our Reskilling for Jobs initiative.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have also created more work trial programmes to help the rank-and-file workers to try out jobs which they may not be familiar or comfortable with.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: After three to six months, they can decide whether to continue.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are also doing much more for the PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We started the year with only 22 PCPs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: By the end of this year, we will have more than 50 PCPs to help many more PMETs to convert to professions and industries with growth potential.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have also provided extra support for mid-career PMETs aged 40 and above.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We believe that they need the extra help.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are doing more for them, especially those who have been unemployed for more than six months.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The Career Support Programme (CSP) was introduced a year ago to help them with wage support.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In response to the questions from Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, we are seeing a higher share of PMETs among residents made redundant.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, 70% of local retrenched workers were PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have, therefore, extended the CSP, since May this year, to two additional groups of PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, we have also extended this CSP to all PMETs made redundant and unable to find jobs after six months, even if they are less than 40 years old.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the younger ones, likewise, we have waived the age requirement as well – after six months of unemployment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our efforts in industry transformation, as outlined by Minister Lim Hng Kiang and Minister Iswaran, will lead to better jobs and better careers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our efforts through SkillsFuture will lead to better workers with deeper skills and newer skills.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And with Adapt and Grow, the focus of MOM is to connect them better to each other – better jobs to better workers; better workers to better jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The National Jobs Bank has been useful in helping our local jobseekers gain access to more jobs, especially PMET jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Today, about 180,000 registered users are gaining access to the Jobs Bank and about 25,700 employers have registered with the Jobs Bank.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At any time, there are about 60,000 active jobs in our Jobs Bank looking for workers and we receive about 7,000 job applications every day.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In response to Dr Tan Wu Meng, we do not intend to make it mandatory for all companies to post all job vacancies in the Jobs Bank and to report all hiring outcomes to MOM, as suggested.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Page: 38 Instead, we will transform the National Jobs Bank into a one-stop and non-stop online marketplace.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It will bring together employers, including those currently not advertising on the Jobs Bank, to bring all their jobs to this marketplace and to connect these employers and their jobs to active and passive jobseekers of all ages.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Jobseekers will be able to explore new career opportunities and conduct job searches on their own through this online marketplace anytime, anywhere without having to wait for the next job fair.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They can be young adults looking for their first jobs, those in mid-careers looking for their next careers, or mature workers looking to remain active.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In response to Mr Desmond Choo, for those who need advice on what jobs and careers to pursue, whether they are current jobseekers or what the Secretary-General of NTUC called "the future jobseekers", such as those vulnerable workers in industries facing poor prospects, we will leverage on the Skills Framework to help them more and serve them better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With the Skills Framework, jobseekers can clearly see what are the career paths, occupations, skills requirements and training programmes available to them in every major sector.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The Skills Frameworks for Hotel and Accommodation Services, and Early Childhood Care and Education have already been launched.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If I may just share this with Members, this is the Skills Framework for the Hotel sector.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With this Skills Framework, you can see clearly there are four career paths for anyone to pursue – from front desk to housekeeping, to sales and marketing, to revenue management.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I asked them what happened to the fifth path, F&B.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They said that would be coming under the F&B Skills Framework.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, any jobseekers can see clearly these are the four plus one-to-come career paths they can pursue.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is how effective the Skills Framework is and will be in the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will be using the Skills Framework, sector by sector, to provide career coaching, counselling to jobseekers to help them discover for themselves which career, job or path is more suitable for them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last, but not least, even salary range is defined in here.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, you see the jobs ladder, skills ladder as well as salary ladder.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And as I have mentioned earlier, the skills framework for two sectors has just been launched and more will come.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: (In Mandarin):   Although local employment is still rising, the speed of growth has slowed down.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we do not adjust our strategy and continue to increase jobs by large numbers, most of the added jobs will be undertaken by foreign employees.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What we are facing now is a slowing economy and a rising redundancy rate.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is the price we have to pay as a result of economic 	Page: 39 transformation in a weak global economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I urge everyone to face this challenge together and persevere.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must make sure that the current difficulties are only short-term transitional pains and not allow them to develop into long-term pains of the new normal.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must assure our SMEs and do our best to help them transform.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: More importantly, we must assure our workers and do our best to help them learn new skills and adapt to new jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Let us work together and quicken our steps to walk out of this transitional period as fast as we can and achieve better and more sustainable economic growth.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This way, everyone will have better jobs, remuneration and career.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: (In English): Madam, in conclusion, as we enter the next stage towards 2%-3% quality growth, I assure our fellow Singaporeans that the tripartite partners are doing our very best for them, at the national as well as sectoral levels.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We need our businesses to do their part, to transform and grow.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, we need our people to do their part, too, to adapt and grow.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last time round, during the Global Financial Crisis, we cut costs together, we saved jobs together, we upturned the downturn together.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This time round, our challenge is to transform together, adapt together, so that we can all grow together.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Working together, I believe that we can succeed once again.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have three questions in the area of strengthening the Singaporean Core, mature PMETs and employment growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The first question is on strengthening the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In our efforts to strengthen the Singaporean Core, perhaps the Minister can give an update on what efforts are being done under the Fair Consideration Framework as well as identifying and handling the "triple weaks" to level the playing field for local PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On the second question about mature PMETs, anecdotally, we still hear of mature PMETs in their 40s and 50s facing challenges in their job search, even when they do relevant training in growth sectors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They feel challenged; sometimes, it could be ageism; sometimes, it could be mindset.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Can MOM, together with our tripartite partners, do even more and do even better in this area?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the exodus of the baby boomers in the coming years and also lower fertility rate and the slower entrance of new workers, does MOM foresee that in the longer term, in five or 10 years' time, we will be able to sustain that one-third to two-thirds local to foreign manpower 	Page: 40 ratio?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We subjected their EP applications to closer scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the last six months, TAFEP has been working very closely with them to improve their HR practices.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Of the 100 companies, about 20%, or one in five, responded by taking part in our job fairs and stepping up training for the locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Some even have knowledge transfer programmes for the locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the remaining 80%, even though many of them have made some improvements, we think that a lot more can be done.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Among them, right now, there are about 300 EP applications still being closely scrutinised, until we are convinced that they have met our fair consideration requirement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, we will continue to identify more of these "triple weak" companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So far, we have identified another 180 of them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The whole purpose is not to punish them, but rather to work with them, engage them and enhance their HR practices to give our Singaporeans fair consideration.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the second point of whether we can do more for the mature PMETs, I would say, certainly, yes.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: More importantly, we are working with more and more companies to open up their job openings to mature workers and to those on the PCP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What we are doing now is, whenever we organise a job fair, whether it is a virtual or physical job fair, the employers will indicate whether they are prepared to take in mature workers for a particular job under CSP or take in workers who are not job-ready but are prepared to go for job conversion under PCP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our intention is to keep growing the list of employers who are prepared to open up more of their jobs under PCP and CSP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In time to come, when the online marketplace is ready, we hope to have a pavilion specially for the mature workers, either on conversion or mid-career switch.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The third question about whether we are able to sustain the one-third to two-thirds local to foreign manpower ratio, right now, we are still about there.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Looking ahead to the next five to 10 years, will we be able to sustain the one-third to two-thirds ratio?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I would say the key consideration is productivity gain.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we are able to strive for the 2%-3% productivity gain, then the pressure on increasing the total workforce would be less.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, I am not able to give you any projection.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But I would say that for now and in the near future, let us focus and apply our mind to innovation and productivity because that is the most sustainable way for us to sustain our growth in the long term without becoming overly dependent on foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recently, I attended a job fair organised by e2i at one of the community centres.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I noticed that employers who had placed jobs were familiar employers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have adopted the suite of programmes the Minister recommended.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we, therefore, nudge them to be more proactive in placing locals and adopting the suite of programmes that he mentioned earlier?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Because for our job fairs in the community, we try to reach out to employers where the jobs are nearby in the community.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Since the companies do not move in and out of communities too quickly, as a result, you are likely to see more of the familiar faces.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Having said that, I do share Mr Ang's concern whether we can keep encouraging more and more companies to step forward, to open up their jobs to our locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The companies are all very keen to look for local workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As I have mentioned, our key challenge is how to connect them better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will continue to organise more and more job fairs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, we want to evolve towards this online marketplace as quickly as possible.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Disruptions in the current job market are intensifying, impacting even the highly trained and younger PMEs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I urge the Minister to put in place measures that give Singaporeans a leg up.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If I may go back to the example highlighted by Mr Iswaran.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Micron has just opened their expanded facility with an investment of a few billion dollars.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For that facility which comes with such a heavy investment, they need to have a few hundred PMETs to keep the place running non-stop.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If MOM were to come in and say, "You have to keep recruiting Singaporeans first until no more Singaporeans would take the jobs before you allow foreigners to take on these jobs", my worry is that if we have that Singaporeans-first reputation, eventually, EDB, MTI, all our agencies will have problems competing for the best investments in the world.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If you look at the EP and at the PMET levels, a vast majority of PMETs in Singapore are local.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Many years from now, we will still have EPs in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I have illustrated earlier to Members that our local workforce growth is slowing down.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, we do need to continue to have foreigners.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Having EP in our system is not a bad thing.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But what is bad is if it leads to unfair consideration for the locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I would say that the best way for us to help the locals is to focus on 	Page: 42 enhancing their employability.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The other point is about retrenchment ‒ whether we can provide incentives for companies to retain locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For companies which retain their locals, we provide a lot of support to them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Earlier, in the Committee of Supply (COS) this year, I announced that we have extended the PCP to in-house PCP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, PMETs, instead of being retrenched, if the company is able to redeploy them within the company, we will support them with the PCP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the whole, I just want to caution that, firstly, retrenchment is not by individuals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Earlier, we talked about a company transferring its R&D operations out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The whole team will be affected, whether you are local or an EP holder, the entire operation will be affected.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: That is why we are concerned that we will see more local PMETs being affected.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: That is the reason why I mentioned earlier we are going to do a lot more to help them to adapt and grow again.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The CSP is obviously a very useful programme for all PMETs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am wondering why restrict the access to the CSP for younger PMETs under 40 years old to only those who are at least unemployed for six months.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why not open CSP to all PMETs, regardless of age?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In helping them, we recognise that some PMETs may need more help than the others.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have observed that the mature PMETs face more challenges.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the mature PMETs, many of them have been working in the industry for 10, 20 years, and their wages are higher.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When they are affected by redundancy, when they move on to another company, to command a similar level of salary is always a big challenge.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As a result, the pay cut that the mature PMETs have to take is normally higher than that for the younger PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The purpose of the CSP is to minimise the wage cut.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our intention is to help these mature PMETs to move to a new company with a new employer, hopefully, without having to suffer too severe a pay cut.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The same may not necessarily apply to the younger PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Here, it is not a case of giving less support to the younger PMETs, but rather giving more support to the mature PMETs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But the strength of a marketplace is also in its centrality.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Will there be incentives for employers across the board to join in, to take part, to make sure that the marketplace is the centre of gravity among the many competing job portals also in the private sector, so that we can have a best source of jobs, a best source of opportunities; a marketplace that is ‒ if I may say ‒ bigger, deeper, better?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our challenge is to make sure that the online marketplace will be attractive to both employers as well as 	Page: 43 jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the employers applying for EPs, they will have to go to the National Jobs Bank.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For them, their presence in the marketplace will be mandatory, through the National Jobs Bank.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For those where the jobs are meant for locals, our aim is to make the online marketplace so attractive that many of them will come on to the marketplace on a voluntary basis.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We believe that, as Dr Tan has mentioned, if we can make this marketplace a vibrant one, a comprehensive one, more and more employers should want to come on board because it would be easier for them to look for the right workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They may have rich experience and so on, so how do we preserve these?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is so that, as a whole, our human capital is preserved and retained so that we can use that to grow our economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, we are also seeing more and more of the mature PMETs now willing to explore opportunities in the SME sector.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
